title: A new deep learning model maps global methane emissions from space.
gist: Google and NASA's JPL published MAPL-EMIT, a deep learning model trained on 3.6 million simulated methane plumes that detects 50% more methane plumes than human experts from NASA's EMIT satellite instrument, and released the resulting global plume database and open-source models/tools publicly.

insights.claim: Google and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory published a peer-reviewed study in PNAS introducing MAPL-EMIT, an AI model that detects and tracks global methane emissions using data from NASA's EMIT (Earth Surface Mineral Dust Source Investigation) instrument.
insights.speaker: Vishal Batchu
insights.so_what: A peer-reviewed, publicly documented model from a Google-NASA collaboration is a credible reference point for AI-driven environmental monitoring capability and for evaluating competing climate-tech satellite analytics vendors.
insights.quote: In a new study published in PNAS, Google and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) introduced MAPL-EMIT, an AI model that tracks methane emissions globally from space using NASA’s EMIT instrument.

insights.claim: MAPL-EMIT was trained on 3.6 million physics-simulated methane plumes to filter out complex, noisy terrain signals, and it detects 50% more methane plumes than human experts, identifying over 23,000 additional plumes globally that had not previously been found.
insights.speaker: Vishal Batchu
insights.so_what: A 50% uplift in plume detection versus human analysts is a concrete, benchmarkable performance claim for AI-based remote sensing — relevant for comparing against other satellite methane-monitoring efforts (e.g., MethaneSAT, Carbon Mapper, GHGSat) on detection recall.
insights.quote: Trained on 3.6 million physics-simulated methane plumes (clouds of methane gas released into the atmosphere), it cuts through complex, noisy terrain to detect 50% more plumes than human experts and identifies more than 23,000 additional plumes globally, including 24 out of 25 of the world’s largest-emitting landfills.

insights.claim: MAPL-EMIT identified 24 of the world's 25 largest-emitting landfills as methane plume sources, indicating landfills are a major, quantifiable, and now more precisely located source of global methane emissions.
insights.speaker: Vishal Batchu
insights.so_what: Precise landfill-level emissions identification creates an actionable target list for waste-management operators, regulators, and carbon-credit/verification businesses to prioritize methane capture or remediation investment.
insights.quote: identifies more than 23,000 additional plumes globally, including 24 out of 25 of the world’s largest-emitting landfills.

insights.claim: Methane has roughly 30 times the warming potential of carbon dioxide over a 100-year timeframe, which is the stated rationale for prioritizing better methane-source detection as a climate mitigation lever.
insights.speaker: Vishal Batchu
insights.so_what: The high per-unit warming potency of methane means targeted detection-and-mitigation (as opposed to broad decarbonization) can deliver outsized near-term climate impact per dollar spent — relevant framing for climate-tech capital allocation.
insights.quote: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas. Over a 100-year timeframe, its warming potential is 30 times greater than that of carbon dioxide.
insights.locator: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas

themes.theme: Open data and tooling release strategy

insights.claim: Google released the global methane plume database generated by MAPL-EMIT on Google Earth Engine along with a visualization app, and made the underlying models open-source on Kaggle with inference tools on GitHub for researchers, policymakers, and operators.
insights.speaker: Vishal Batchu
insights.so_what: By open-sourcing both the dataset and inference tools rather than gating them, Google is positioning Earth Engine and its climate-data infrastructure as the default public layer for methane monitoring, which could crowd out or complement commercial methane-monitoring startups depending on how they build on it.
insights.quote: Google has released the global plume database on Earth Engine alongside an Earth Engine app to visualize the data. Open-source models are available on Kaggle and inference tools are on GitHub to support researchers, policymakers, and operators.
insights.locator: Google has released the global plume database
